subject: Climate & Environment
title: Methane: The Silent Threat
description: A fast breakdown of Methane: The Silent Threat for builders.

hook.text: Methane traps 80 times more heat than CO₂ over 20 years. It just fades faster.

buildup.text: Cows belch it. Rice paddies bubble it. Landfills leak it into the air constantly.

discovery.text: Natural gas is mostly methane — and pipelines leak far more than anyone expected.

twist.text: Scientists found methane plumes so large they are visible from satellites in orbit.

climax.text: Cutting methane is the fastest way to slow warming because it disappears in a decade.

punchline.text: The fastest climate win is plugging leaks we already know about.

quiz.question: How does methane compare to CO₂ in heat-trapping power over 20 years?

details.summary: Methane is a greenhouse gas over 80 times more potent than CO2 over 20 years, responsible for roughly 30 percent of warming since pre-industrial times. Major sources include livestock, rice paddies, oil and gas leaks, landfills, and thawing permafrost.
details.whyItMatters: Methane's short atmospheric lifetime of about 12 years means cutting it delivers fast climate benefits. It is the single fastest lever for slowing near-term warming.
takeaways: Methane is 80 times more potent than CO2 over 20 years
It breaks down in about 12 years, unlike centuries for CO2
Cutting methane is the fastest way to slow warming this decade

faq.question: Why is methane called a short-lived climate pollutant?
faq.answer: Methane breaks down in the atmosphere in about 12 years through oxidation. This short lifetime means that reducing methane emissions leads to measurable concentration drops within a decade, unlike CO2 which persists for centuries.

faq.question: How much methane leaks from the oil and gas industry?
faq.answer: Satellite data and ground measurements suggest the oil and gas sector leaks 70 to 80 million tons of methane annually, far more than industry self-reports. Much of this leakage could be stopped cost-effectively with existing technology.
